title: For God so loved (John 3:9–21)
hook: the most famous verse: God so loved the world
carry: not to condemn but to save

segments.voice: Yesterday, anothen: born again, or born from above. Your line was the wind blows where it will. Six hundred days on the path.

You've probably seen it without reading it. On a sign at a football game. On the bottom of a fast-food cup. On an athlete's eye black. Just a reference: John three sixteen. For many people it's the one Bible verse they could find without looking it up, which makes it easy to stop hearing. Today it goes back where it lives, in a night conversation with a confused teacher named Nicodemus, next to the verse hardly anyone puts on a sign.

Nicodemus is still asking, how can these things be? Jesus reaches for a story he knew well. In the wilderness, when the people were dying of snakebite, Moses lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived. "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up." In John, lifted up means two things: raised on a cross, and raised in glory. Then the famous lines: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved." Notice two things. First, the little word so. In Greek it's houtōs, and many scholars point out it means in this way more than so much: God loved the world by giving. Second, the world. John's word is kosmos, and in his Gospel the world is often the part of creation that has turned away from God. That's what God loved. Not the lovable parts. The world. Then verse seventeen, the one rarely painted on signs: not to condemn, but to save. One honest note: Greek has no quotation marks, so nobody knows exactly where Jesus's words end and John's reflection begins here, and red-letter Bibles disagree. Christians read these verses as the whole Gospel in miniature: love that gives, aimed at a world that doesn't deserve it.
screen: then, large: `FOR GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Find John three sixteen and seventeen, or just listen to them in your head, and read sixteen slowly, out loud if you can, then seventeen just as slowly. Let the second verse sit beside the first, and hold one part of the world you find hardest to love, a person, a group, a place, inside those two verses for a moment.
Kosmos, the Greek word for the world, the ordered universe — John's word for what God loved in this way, by giving his Son, not to condemn, but to save.
Your line: not to condemn but to save. It's the verse that rarely makes the sign. Six hundred days, done.

howItsDone: John 3:16 is among the first verses many Christians memorize as children, and many churches read John 3:14–21 in Lent, pairing it with the story of the bronze serpent in Numbers 21.

chat.says: John 3:16 is everywhere. Is it really about God loving the whole world, or just good people?
options: The whole world, even the part turned away, and God sent his Son to save it, not condemn it.
It's about people who earn God's love by being good first, and then believe.
Read the next verse: God sent his Son mainly to condemn the world.
chat.meaning: John's kosmos is often the world turned away from God, and that's what God loved, sending his Son not to condemn but to save.

notes: οὕτως as 'in this way' rather than 'so much': argued by a number of commentators; others hold it includes degree. Phrased as 'many scholars point out'. Confirm.
κόσμος in John often negative (e.g. 1:10; 15:18). Confirm.
Uncertain end of Jesus's speech in John 3 (after 3:15 or 3:21): standard. Confirm.
